:::{#def-empirical-distribution}
#### Empirical distribution

For observed values $\dsn{x}$,
the **empirical distribution** is the distribution of a value
[chosen at random](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-random-choice)
from the sample,
each of the $n$ observations being equally likely:
the probability that the value falls in a set $A$ is

$$\frac{1}{n}\sumjn \indicp{x_j \in A}.$$

:::

:::{#exm-empirical-distribution}
#### Numerical example: empirical distribution

Suppose the observed values are $4, 1, 7, 3$, so $n = 4$,
and let $A = [2, 5)$.
Two of the four values (4 and 3) lie in $A$,
so the empirical distribution gives $A$ probability $2/4 = 0.5$.
Each observed value has probability $1/4$,
and any set containing none of them has probability $0$.
:::

::: {.remark .notes}

#### What "empirical" means

"Empirical" means computed from the observed data,
not from a model or a population.
An empirical quantity is the matching population quantity
with the
[population distribution](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-population-distribution)
replaced by the empirical distribution.
For example,
the mean of the empirical distribution is the
[sample mean](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-sample-mean),
and its CDF is the [empirical CDF](#def-empirical-cdf).
Machine learning uses the same replacement
to turn the risk of a prediction model into its *empirical risk*.

Because it needs only the data in hand,
an empirical quantity can always be computed,
and it serves as an estimate of the population quantity it mimics.
The bootstrap rests on this replacement:
it estimates the variability of a statistic
by sampling from the empirical distribution
[@hastie2009elements, section 7.11, p. 250; @efron1993introduction].

:::
